before.descent_text: The usual descent is the southwest ridge, the hikers' route, which leads down to Moraine Lake.

before.approach: The main approach goes from the Kain hut or Applebee campground over the Bugaboo-Snowpatch Col, then northwest down the Vowell Glacier beneath the north ridge to the North Shoulder Col. Descend west into the steep, loose gully, skirt the small glacier below the northwest face on its right, and scree and glacier lead south to the foot of the west face. The alternative is the East Creek basin: take the ridge toward the middle tower, then rappel to the glacier below and cross the cirque. Either way is long and remote, with rockfall off the north face above the cirque. The route starts from the ledges where the lower wall pushes furthest into the glacier.
before.descent_text: The route ends on the summit ridge, a long stretch of fourth-class climbing with the odd harder move. The descent is by rappel down the east face, on anchors that range from pitons to slung horns and shift from year to year; the rock is very loose. Below the bergschrund, rappel or downclimb to the glacier, avoiding crevasses, and walk out.

before.approach: The main approach goes from the Kain hut or Applebee campground over the Bugaboo-Snowpatch Col, then northwest down the Vowell Glacier beneath the north ridge to the North Shoulder Col. Descend west into the steep, loose gully, skirt the small glacier below the northwest face on its right, and scree and glacier lead south to the foot of the west face. The East Creek basin is the other way in, with bolted rappels down to the base. Look for a corner crack that is wide at the back and has a hand-width splitter on its right side, a little left of where the west face comes lowest.
before.descent_text: The route ends on the summit ridge. The descent is by rappel down the east face just below the summit, to below the bergschrund and then a short downclimb to the glacier. The east face is very loose, the old rappel anchors may need replacing, and ropes can snag.

before.approach: The main approach goes from the Kain hut or Applebee campground over the Bugaboo-Snowpatch Col, then northwest down the Vowell Glacier beneath the north ridge to the North Shoulder Col. Descend west into the steep, loose gully, skirt the small glacier below the northwest face on its right, and scree and glacier lead south to the foot of the west face, where this route climbs to the right of the older lines. The alternative is the East Creek basin and its rappels, which is a lot of work.

The wall is reached from Crescent Meadow near Moro Rock by a long backcountry hike to Hamilton Lake, the nearest camp. A backcountry permit is required and overnight stays at the lake are limited. The south face of Angel Wings rises directly above the lake basin. The route climbs the south face by a crack system of wide grooves, beside the Rowell-Jones line and just left of it.

The wall is reached from Crescent Meadow near Moro Rock by a long backcountry hike to Hamilton Lake, the nearest camp. A backcountry permit is required and overnight stays at the lake are limited. The south face of Angel Wings rises directly above the lake basin. The route starts in the centre of the main south face, on the left-hand one of two crossing ramps whose X shape is visible a few hundred feet up.

Follow the Bubbs Creek trail east from Road's End at Cedar Grove, the same long hike used for Charlotte Dome, to the camping area just beyond the Charlotte Creek crossing. Continue a short way along the trail until the big wall comes into view on the left. The route begins at a large pine a little uphill and to the right of the enormous white dihedral that opens the crystal band.

Drive the Mineral King road to the Paradise Ridge trailhead, close to Atwell Mill campground. Hike the Paradise Ridge trail up to the ridge, then leave it and contour north-northwest cross-country, threading a few minor drainages, until the Fortress, and the gully under it, appear ahead; the whole way in is roughly six miles. Stay on the right (east) side of the gully until below the wall, cross it, and climb to the base. The line follows a corner and offwidth system on the east face.

before.descent_text: Parties descend by rappelling the route. The upper pitches have fixed belay stations that make the first rappels straightforward, but at the big bivouac ledge the rappel line leaves the climbing line and drops down the face to the right of the chimneys, on bolted anchors that start at the northeast end of the ledge and reach the top of the third pitch. Anchors on the headwall are worth noting on the way up, because the stations on the lower face are hard to find from above. Stay out of the chimney: ropes snag on every feature there and the descent becomes slow. From the top of the third pitch a further rappel reaches the top of the first.

before.approach: Start at the Summit Lake shelter and travel up the Caribou Glacier toward the Caribou/Parade divide, heading north-west. Beyond the divide you reach the Parade Glacier by one of two ways: steep snow and ice down the west edge, or a rappel from the bolted anchor by the saddle on the east. The climb starts on the East Face just right of an obvious deep gully above the Parade Glacier; the wall across from that gully sheds rock, so do not linger beneath it.
before.descent_text: The route ends on the summit plateau of the North Tower, and the standard way down starts from an obvious rappel point across the plateau. Rappels lead down to the gap separating the two towers, then a rotten gully leads to a hanging snowfield whose crossing is exposed and may be icy. Beyond it you can scramble or keep rappelling slabs and cliffs from established anchors. The anchors on the standard route are of modest quality, and rockfall in the gully is a hazard. Rappelling the route itself is possible but most of the lower face has no anchors, so it means setting your own down a very tall wall.

before.approach: Park at the pullout on the westbound Trans-Canada Highway about halfway between the Mount Norquay turnoff and the Bow Valley Parkway turnoff. Cross the animal fence at the runoff channel and follow the channel briefly, then climb the ridge on the right under the power lines, using a faint trail through burned timber to the crest. Follow the ridge to a col, bear right onto the ridge beyond it, and where a slab blocks the way drop left past a cairn through a wooded stretch and scree gully. Follow the clifftop to an opening where the upper slab is straight ahead. Calamari Crack climbs the corner just right of Escargot Corner.

Park at the pullout on the westbound Trans-Canada Highway about halfway between the Mount Norquay turnoff and the Bow Valley Parkway turnoff. Cross the animal fence at the runoff channel and follow the channel briefly, then climb the ridge on the right under the power lines, using a faint trail through burned timber to the crest. Follow the ridge to a col, bear right onto the ridge beyond it, and where a slab blocks the way drop left past a cairn through a wooded stretch and scree gully. Follow the clifftop to an opening where the upper slab is straight ahead. Escargot Corner follows the leftmost right-facing corner of the upper slab.
before.descent_text: From the top-out ledge walk up and left, then up and right onto the ridge system. Follow the ridge to a sharp drop, where a boulder wrapped in a black chain serves as the rappel anchor, and rappel to easier ground. Then scramble down the ridge to the approach trail.

before.approach: Prindle is reached by a rough road from Fairbanks that suits a high-clearance four-wheel-drive vehicle, followed by a long approach to the base of the main climbing areas. Razorback is a small cragging formation tucked between the Southeast Buttress and the East Tower; the lines sit on its right-hand face as you hike up from below. Razorbutt is a short wide crack reached by hiking up the hillside and around to the back of the formation.

Prindle is reached by a rough road from Fairbanks that suits a high-clearance four-wheel-drive vehicle, followed by a long approach to the base of the main climbing areas. Head to the Main Wall; the Southeast Buttress is the feature on its right. Homewrecker starts in the low-angle grassy gully at the middle of the toe of the buttress, where most parties scramble the first pitch to a bolted station off to the left of the ramp.
before.descent_text: A rappel anchor on the far side of the tower drops you into the gully. Single-rope rappels with a long rope work, with some fourth class downscrambling between; a large boulder with slings marks the next rappel station, which finishes in the bottom of the Keyhole.

before.approach: Cali Slit is in the Spirit Boulder Area at the Mile High Wall in the Reed Lakes basin of Hatcher Pass. Drive from Palmer up North Palmer Fishhook Road to the Mother Lode Lodge switchback, then onto Archangel Road, and walk the trail to the abandoned cabin where the climbing begins. The area lies left of the approach gully to the Shield, Main Wall and Two Toke Tower, and the route starts left of the Spirit Boulder Chalice.

Park where the guardrail ends just past the 17 mile sign on the road out of Haines. Drop into the ditch and follow the creek past the culvert to a flagged trail into the woods, which leads to a boulder field. Go straight up to the wall, or take the trail up the right side of the boulder field to avoid loose rock and moss; it reaches the base of Chest Fur. Unnamed 4 is the obvious overhanging crack as you work right along the wall.

From the meadow camp, climb to the col between the Deacon and the Matriarch, then follow the ridgeline toward the Deacon and drop onto snow and talus to the foot of the north-east wall. Sentinel Direct starts at the V-shaped feature on the left side of the wall.

From the meadow camp, climb to the col between the Deacon and the Matriarch, then follow the ridgeline toward the Deacon and drop onto snow and talus to the foot of the north-east wall. The Heretic starts at the V-shaped feature on the left side of the wall, shared with Sentinel Direct.
before.descent_text: The route finishes on easy ground, then scrambles to the summit. Scramble along the ridge, then step off it ahead of the loose, blocky towers; one short rappel leads to a traverse across and up through chossy rock that is gentler and less exposed than the towers. From the summit, follow the ridgeline down. Cornices build over the gullies, so do not shortcut across early-season snow.

before.approach: Approach up the lower Vowell Glacier into the cirque, then angle right to the start on the east side of the ridge. Easy scrambling leads to where the technical climbing begins.
before.descent_text: The route tops out on the third summit of the ridge. Rappel down the ridgeline to the glacier; do not count on fixed anchors, so carry gear to build your own. Retreat off either face is difficult, so avoid the route if storms are likely.

before.approach: Start from the Glacier Gorge trailhead and follow the trail past Loch Vale. Just beyond the lake, turn right onto the Andrew's Glacier trail; the split comes right after a creek crossing and is easy to miss. Follow that trail to just short of the Andrew's campground sign, where a faint path turns hard left and uphill into The Gash, a large boulder field. Sharkstooth appears on the left; work up through the boulders, staying low near the glacial runoff, to the base of the ridge. Raptor closures can apply to this part of the park in spring and early summer, so check current park closures.
before.descent_text: From the summit, head southeast down a gully to the first rappel anchors, following cairns. Bolted stations lead down in three rappels, after which a class 3 downclimb reaches the top of The Gash, and you return by the approach. The descent is the same line used by the East Gully route. Rockfall is the main hazard, so call out when pulling ropes, and check each anchor before trusting it, since some old pins and webbing remain.

before.approach: The usual way in is the Spanish Creek trail, which starts at the Crestone Mountain Zen Center's upper parking lot on private land, so the landowner's rules apply and a wilderness access permit is needed. The trail follows Spanish Creek and crosses it several times, with a blowdown section and cairns. Camp near treeline below the lower buttress of the Prow. The Prow is a fin on the southwest ridge of Kit Carson. Stay on the east side of it while approaching to avoid getting cliffed out.
before.descent_text: From the top, where a large ledge gives access to Kit Carson and Challenger Point, walk east over another peak to the broad low valley between Kit Carson and Ellingwood, which leads back toward camp. Do not turn down too early, because that line meets steep slabs.

before.approach: Follow the Wolf's Head trail where it splits off to the south of Pingora, then work along the base of the formation on a slabby, flower-covered ramp. A little class 4 traversing leads to the start, which sits directly beneath the thumb-shaped spire on the wall.
before.descent_text: Descend by rappel. The rappels are long and need two long ropes. Loose blocks and flakes near the stations make pulling the ropes risky, so clear the lines and watch for snags.

before.approach: The usual way in is from the east, starting at the Pine Creek Pass trailhead. Follow the trail past Upper Pine Lake, bend toward Honeymoon Lake and continue into Granite Park, then cross Granite Bear Pass near 12,400 feet. West of the pass, go between Big Bear Lake (to the north) and Little Bear Lake (to the south), trend southwest past a few tarns to Vee Lake, and follow the stream flowing out of it to the East Fork of Bear Creek. From there, climb cross-country up to the east side of the peak. Navigation off the trail needs care.

Reach Miter Basin over Cottonwood Pass, Old or New Army Pass, or Arc Pass; the Cottonwood way is the longer, gentler two-day option with a camp at Chicken Spring Lake, while crossing Old Army Pass from Horseshoe Meadows and dropping to Soldier Lake is the shorter, harder one. Camp anywhere in the basin. The Sky Blue Diamond stands directly south of Sky Blue Lake, the fourth formation counting from the south end of the group. Altared State starts to the right of the A-frame crack that splits the headwall. Scramble up from the base to a large ledge running across the right side of the formation, with one short fourth-class move, and start from there.
before.descent_text: Reverse the upper pitches to the descent ledge above the Diamond, using a series of downclimbs and a couple of rappels. Alternatively, from the big ledge reached after the fourth pitch, a non-technical walk-off leads north back toward the base; continuing to the summit means the technical way back to that ledge.

From the May Lake trailhead, either make a rising traverse across from the lake or follow a faint, unmaintained trail to the foot of the cliffs and climb straight up. The buttress lies north-northeast of the lake and the orange rock is easy to spot. Clean Living starts at a vertical crack system about midway between Taphophobia and Fear of Flying.

From the May Lake trailhead, either make a rising traverse across from the lake or follow a faint, unmaintained trail to the foot of the cliffs and climb straight up. The buttress lies north-northeast of the lake and the orange rock is easy to spot. Pure Thoughts starts from the corner at the base of Taphophobia: belay there, then step right and head up the flakes.

From the May Lake trailhead, either make a rising traverse across from the lake or follow a faint, unmaintained trail to the foot of the cliffs and climb straight up. The buttress lies north-northeast of the lake and the orange rock is easy to spot. Fear of Fun starts about twenty feet left of The Astraphobia Treatment.

Park at the pullouts on Highway 120 (Tioga Road) just over half a mile east of Ellery Lake dam, or use the Warren Creek trailhead area nearby, and climb the broken slabs above the road straight up to the base of the ridge. The first climbing is a steep, loose dihedral.

The wall stands directly above Spring Lake at the head of Cliff Creek Canyon, in the backcountry of Sequoia and Kings Canyon, and every way in starts at the Mineral King road end. The usual line is to hike to Monarch Lake and cross Glacier Pass into the basin; the other choice is to go over Timber Gap and then follow Cliff Creek up to the lake. Spring Roll begins at the toe of the left-most of the three formations that make up the wall.
before.descent_text: Walk off the back of the formation, skier's left, heading down toward Cyclamen Lake. A short rappel from a slung boulder into a steep gully may be needed; staying higher and further left may allow a scramble instead. Continue left and down through the slabs to return to Spring Lake. Another option is to go on up to the top of the main formation and descend by its line.

before.approach: The Paradise Ridge trailhead sits off the Mineral King road, near Atwell Mill; hike that trail up to the ridge crest. From there go cross-country north-northwest, contouring across minor drainages until the Fortress wall, with its gully below, shows ahead. Keep to the gully's east (right) bank until you are beneath the wall, then step across and scramble up to the foot of the rock. The Sage is the left-most route on the wall.

Start on the Tuttle Creek trail and walk to the stone landmark called the Ashram, then bear left along a sandy sidehill path to reach the south fork of the creek and follow that drainage uphill. The path fades past the Ashram, so watch for cairns. Some way up, the Tuttle Creek Obelisk appears above on the right; keep going until the creek runs directly beneath the Basecamp Wall below the Obelisk. The wall is clean, with camping and water at its foot. An overnight wilderness permit is needed to camp in Tuttle Creek.

Leave the car at the pack station where the Pine Creek road ends and take the Pine Creek Pass trail uphill; the Brownstone Mine wall appears on the left, a short step off the trail, so no off-trail travel is needed. The trail is sunny even though the wall is shaded, so an early start helps, and early in the season there are several creek crossings with little water at the crag itself. Alpine Creek is one of the longer lines in the Upper Brownstone section of the crag.

This is a remote north-facing buttress in a valley just south of Walk of Life Spire. From the pond and meadow below the scree field under that spire, follow the side valley that splits off to the south all the way back to the foot of The Stargate. The line follows the weakness just left of the centre of the buttress.
before.descent_text: From the top, traverse east to the north-facing chute just east of the climb and descend it into the valley below.

before.approach: From Jasper, drive toward Hinton and turn onto the road to Miette Hot Springs. A viewpoint on that road shows the ridge and is a good place to study the routes. Beyond the hairpin turn, leave the car in a small left-hand pullout and take the faint path that drops to the river. Cross the river at the right spot, which is usually about knee deep outside spring and wet weather. On the far side, go left to the break in the first big cliff band, then trend right and scramble through two smaller bands, using faint forest trails where you can find them; much of this is bushwhacking.

Start from the Castle Mountain fire lookout and head north, uphill, on a trail that gets steeper to a gully, cross the drainage heading east and pick the trail up again. It continues steeply to the bottom of the hut access trail, where rappel bolts show above. From there go left, to the west, a short way to a bowl-shaped wall; the first-pitch bolts are easy to see.
before.descent_text: The simplest way off is to walk: from the top, head east across the plateau toward the Castle Mountain hut, then descend the hut access trail, which has a few short fourth-class downclimbs and an optional rappel, back to the base of the wall and the lookout. Belay anchors on the route are fixed for rappelling.

before.approach: Take the Rockbound Lake trail to the turnoff for the Lost Lemon crag, continue a short way farther, then head up and left through forest to a drainage. The prow of the route is obvious once you reach the wall.
before.descent_text: From the upper anchor, traverse the ledge to the right: a steep hike above the lower cliff band, with bolts for the first stretch if you want to stay roped. The second half is lower-angled; stay high until you can curve around the corner onto the east side and pick up the trail back down.

before.approach: The trailhead is a roadside pullout on Highway 16 east of Jasper, on the right when heading toward Jasper from Hinton, just past a bridge, and a garbage bin marks it. Walk from the back of the pullout onto the established hiking trail to Cinquefoil Mountain, and stay on it until the crag shows ahead. Where the path splits faintly short of a rounded rise, bear right, then follow the switchbacks and cross a meadow to the foot of the cliff.

Park in the small roadside pullout just before the bridge on Highway 16, where wooden signs point toward Roche Ronde and Smet. Across the road, climb the obvious trail up the left side of a blasted cliff face, and at the first fork take the faint left branch, which is easy to miss; you are on the right trail when you walk along a grassy ridge with gentle drops on both sides. Follow it up to a marked ridge, which is the top of the wall, then continue to a pair of small spruce trees beside a cairn, where the climbers' trail starts. It passes a downward scramble protected by wire cable and reaches the base of the wall, with the obvious face on your left and low first bolts.

Park at the pullout on the west side of the Icefields Parkway by Hector Creek and pick up the Mount Hector trail on the south side of the drainage. It runs through forest, along the left edge of an avalanche bowl and on to the lip of a waterfall. Cross the creek there into the small hanging valley between Andromache and Little Hector, then follow cairns and goat trails up a series of benches and an easy gully to the upper benches. Cross left over a bowl with a big boulder, follow the dry watercourse to the base of the towers and continue to the farthest-left bowl. The right-hand tower is easily mistaken for the spire. The route starts below and left of a big black roof, at a one-bolt station on a small ledge.
before.descent_text: Rappel the route on fixed anchors, using a 60 m rope; the first rappel is from the summit ring-bolts. Two of the stations are reached by short walks or scrambles along ledges, and one long rappel is overhanging with a stiff pull, so knot the rope ends. At the foot of the route, follow the cairns back down the approach to the highway.

before.approach: Drive Maligne Lake Road to the pullout near the two boulders on the left, beyond the picnic area on the right. From there a trail climbs past a boulder field to the slab.

From Jasper, take the Icefields Parkway south to Athabasca Falls, take the old highway (93A) there, and continue past the falls to Leech Lake. Park in the pullout there, or in the small one a little farther on the left. A well-kept trail leads into the forest and reaches the crag in a short walk.

Take Maligne Lake Road from Highway 16 east of Jasper and park at the bridge pullout on the left. Cross the bridge, turn left into the forest in the direction of the next bridge, and shortly turn right onto the marked trail that climbs a steep hill. Where the marked trail veers right, keep left on an unmarked trail and follow it through open Douglas fir forest until a drop-off appears on your left. Turn right and go downhill to reach Rock Gardens; going downhill and left leads to Boulder Gardens instead.

Park in the large pullout on Highway 16 near the Hidden Valley lot, with an outhouse nearby, and start along the trail at the east end of the Hidden Valley parking area. A small pond may need crossing on logs. The trail braids into goat paths and then turns up the valley; follow the orange flagging, small rock cages and cairns toward the base of the cliff. The first few routes begin on the first buttress; continue along the cliff line past an obvious wide break to the second buttress, which holds most of the routes.

Park in the round, sandy pullout on the Icefields Parkway south of the Kerkeslin campground entrance. Behind it, pass through a gap in the trees into a small hidden field and head toward Kerkeslin crag, taking the narrow trail that bears slightly right through poplar forest, where it steepens. Shortly after leaving the aspens, take the fork to the left; if you can already see short cliffs ahead before turning, you have gone too far, so go back a short way to the fork. The new trail then follows a creek up a narrow canyon to the walls.

Drive the Snaring road past the campsites to where it turns to dirt; after the big U-turn above Jasper Lake the crag is on the left as the road descends, and parking is on the right by the open field. Walk up the powerline line to the second pole, then a little farther on angle right up scrambly ground to top out the lower, chossy cliff band. The routes are on the obvious low-angle slabs above it, on sharp rock.
before.descent_text: The anchors sit well back from the top of the climbs, so lowering drags the rope across the rock and wears it.

Drop into the ditch, follow the creek past the culvert, and pick up the flagged trail that climbs into the woods to a boulder field. For the Bear Spray Wall, leave the main trail and head up and to the right until you meet a second flagged trail, which passes several small loose cliffs before reaching the wall.

Drive up Red Rock Canyon to about halfway, past the large red debris pile nearest the road, and park at one of the pullouts beyond it. Find the prominent ridge running up to the canyon rim and climb it with only a short bit of bushwhacking to the west rim, then cross the tundra plateau to the east rim. The crags sit at the top of the plateau just to the south, nearer Canwell Peak.

Thumb Cove is on the east side of Resurrection Bay, south of Seward, and is reached by paddle, motorboat or water taxi from town. Check tides, weather and the marine forecast before going. Some undeveloped parts of the cove have difficult foot access.

That trail runs to the largest meadow, where it meets a creek you do not cross; take the beaten path across the meadow to the cairn on the rise before the trees, then keep to the well-worn trail up to the big meadow below the bowl. The climbers' trail crosses that meadow straight to the base of Lower Replica. From there, follow the trail up and right alongside the cliff to the scree field between Lower and Upper Replica, cross it, pass below Upper Replica to a second short scree field, and continue up and left. The first route you reach is Boy Scout Hand Grenade; the rest sit on a small treed ledge a bit farther up the slope.

The Main Wall faces southwest and gets sun all day.

From the ski area, park in the upper lot behind the lodge and walk up the paved McCollister Road toward the Union Pass lift. Where the pavement stops a small trail leaves to the left; it meets a service road, which you follow left until it turns into a steep trail climbing to the buttress. Climbers using the tram instead descend by the Rock Springs Loop trail along the ridge opposite Cody Peak, bear left on the road at the first junction, take the trail down to the next junction and turn right toward the ski trails, then pick up a cairned climbers' trail on the right that drops to the base. The West Sector is the far-left crag after the creek, on the talus field, with a steep gully on its right, and it is the first crag reached when coming down from the tram.

before.approach: Drive northeast on Hinkey Summit Road past the pass and park well off the road in a wider spot. Hike northwest on cattle paths through the sagebrush and across a small boulder field to reach the middle of the wall.

Pull off into the small parking spot on the left side of Hinkey Summit Road, short of the bend. Walk up the road a short way to two cairns on the right marking the trail, then head north-northeast on the best cow trail across the hillside. Cross Indian Creek at the stick-and-rock cairn by a large Y-shaped dead snag, then follow cow and climber trails along the treeline northeast until the wall appears over the crest. The west side of the formation is the steeper, pocketed face; the south side is lower angle.

From the upper climbers' camp, take the trail down across Forest Service Road 850 and climb the Lookout Ridge Trail until just short of the crest of the Panorama Point knoll, where a side trail leaves on the left onto the point (Rabbit Ears is close by to the south); follow it down the left (back) side of the point to the base of the cliff.

Park where the seasonal road from Route 108 ends and walk up the road; the cliffs stand on both sides of it. The buttress is a clean wall just south of the Quartz Crack Face. Starting at Quartz Crack, contour north (to the right, facing the rock) and a little downhill past The Diagonal to a low-angle bolted slab, with the climbs just right of the herd path. Other ways in: climb south on the herd path out of ENT Gully, or head straight up from the top of the Smugglers' Notch lot past Biscuit.

Drive up Little Cottonwood Canyon to Tanners Campground and park on the large shoulder on the east side just past it, before the bend. Behind the Tanners Slide Path sign across the highway a trail leads down to the drainage; follow it into the gulch and walk up the drainage (the west side of the stream seems to have the better trail). Look for the first pronounced gully on the left, Witches and Divas; the east-facing wall is on the right side of that gully. The upper gulch is steep with loose talus, and it is avalanche terrain in winter and spring, so check the avalanche forecast.

Park at the Crystal Lake trailhead and follow the trail toward Wall Lake, crossing the bridge east over the outlet. Climb the switchbacks above Wall Lake to Hope Lake, follow its east side to the pass, go by Lake Lovenia and descend switchbacks to Ibantik Lake. The north-facing wall is south of the lake: walk up talus on the west side and skirt the base of the cliff to your route.

Park at the Lofty Lake trailhead, beyond the Mirror Lake turnoff, on the left if you drove from Kamas. Follow the Weber River Trail west to a fork and take the left branch, then leave the trail to the left toward Reids Peak. There is no trail from there: pick your way to the talus field below the wall and work up it to the base.

Follow the approach to the Shattered Sea (see that crag), then keep going toward the cliff edge. The trail skirts the edge over broken rock and short cliffs, then slopes downhill and opens out with less deadfall. When the ground begins to rise again, watch for a cluster of cairns on your right by some pines, which mark the crag top. The base is reached by a short, steep talus chute, which is best roped.

A cairned trail then continues southeast to the crag, though it can be hard to follow in places. The north entrance to the crag is marked by two cairns.
